title: Concentration Inequalities and Martingale Inequalities: A Survey
abstractRaw: We examine a number of generalized and extended versions of concentration inequalities and martingale inequalities. These inequalities are effective for analyzing processes with quite general conditions as illustrated in an example for an infinite Polya process and web graphs.

title: Anhedonia and Emotional Processing of Past- and Future-Directed Mental Representations: Behavioral and Event-Related Potential Evidence
authors: Matthias Pillny, Kai Härpfer, Hannes Per Carsten, Anja Riesel, Julia Klawohn, Tania Marie Lincoln
abstractRaw: Anhedonia may involve difficulties generating affective value from remembered and imagined positive experiences rather than a generalized reduction in immediate pleasure. However, its association with emotional processing across direct stimulus exposure, memory retrieval, and prospection, including the role of negative affect, remain unclear. This preregistered study examined neural and subjective emotional responses in 48 nonclinical adults with varying levels of anhedonia. Participants viewed positive, negative, and neutral images, recalled them, and imagined future experiences involving their content. During 4,000-ms trials, late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes were assessed from 400 to 4,000 ms, alongside subjective affect and imagery vividness ratings. Anhedonia was assessed using the Snaith–Hamilton Pleasure Scale. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between anhedonia and LPP amplitudes across valence conditions and time windows, as well as subjective ratings across valence conditions. During recall, higher anhedonia was associated with reduced positive–neutral LPP differentiation at 1,000–2,000 and 2,000–3,000 ms, alongside lower pleasantness ratings for positive memories. Valence-dependent LPP associations were not significant during encoding or prospection. These findings suggest that altered affective processing of positive memories may be relevant to anhedonia, alongside broader differences in emotional responding and the vividness of mental representations.

title: Neural Correlates of Partner Comparisons and Their Links to Intimate Partner Aggression
authors: Sydney Kavanaugh, Alexandra Martelli, Samuel J. West, Emily Lasko, David Chester
abstractRaw: People frequently compare themselves to their intimate partners. These partner comparisons are critical for relationship maintenance, with powerful ramifications for intimate partner aggression (IPA) perpetration. However, little is known about the neural correlates of partner comparisons and their relation to IPA perpetration. To address this gap, 96 participants from 49 intimate partner dyads underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and completed a social comparison task, judging their own negative and positive traits against those of their partner and the average person. Participants then reported whether they had any history of IPA perpetration. Consistent with previous findings, participants reported having less negative and more positive traits than others. However, participants’ tendency to compare themselves favorably to others was attenuated for their partners. Partner (> average person) comparisons were linked to heightened activity in the mentalizing network (DMPFC, precuneus, TPJ) and DLPFC, particularly for negative traits. Such DLPFC/DMPFC activity during partner comparisons related to greater IPA perpetration for negative traits and lesser IPA perpetration for positive traits. These findings suggest that recruiting mentalizing and executive control networks during partner comparisons may be meaningfully linked to IPA perpetration, depending on trait valence.

title: Examining associations between brain volume and alexithymia in autistic youth and young adults
authors: Goldie A McQuaid, Gregory Wallace, Alex Job Said, Stefen Beeler-Duden, Zachary Jacokes, Kevin Pelphrey, Allison Jack
abstractRaw:
Alexithymia is a dimensional trait including challenges labeling emotions. Alexithymia is elevated in autistic individuals relative to the general population and is suggested to be part of the broader autism phenotype. Alexithymia is also independently associated with emotion regulation challenges, which are more prevalent among autistic persons, and with two of the most common co-occurring conditions among autistic people: depression and anxiety. A better understanding of alexithymia, including its neural correlates, therefore promises to advance our understanding of risk profiles for mental health problems in autistic people.

We therefore sought to: 1) characterize alexithymia in autistic (n=54) and neurotypical (n=56) adolescents and young adults (15-25y) including group and sex differences; 2) examine group and sex differences in brain volume in eight regions of interest implicated in alexithymia; and 3) explore potential interactions between group and brain volume as predictors of alexithymia.

Autistic individuals self-reported significantly higher levels of alexithymia relative to neurotypical individuals, with autistic females reporting the highest levels and neurotypical males the lowest levels. There were no differences in group or sex based on brain volume. Exploratory models predicting alexithymia found a significant interaction between group and right dorsal anterior cingulate cortex volume.

title: Regulating Self-Interest: The Effect of Anodal tDCS over the Right Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex in the Ultimatum Game
authors: Haim Assor, Jonathan Slater, Eliran Halali
abstractRaw: In many social situations, a conflict exists between self-interest and social considerations such as fairness and reciprocity. Previous research suggests that self-interested behavior is an automatic response, requiring cognitive control to be regulated. Consistent with this view, neuroeconomics findings implicate the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) in regulating self-interested behavior and implementing social preferences. Whereas prior neuromodulation studies have shown that inhibition or disruption of the rDLPFC increases self-interested behavior, studies examining the effects of enhancing rDLPFC activity have yielded inconsistent results. Moreover, it remains unclear whether such enhancement promotes responses to intentional unfairness alone or also to inequality per se. In the present study, we applied anodal transcranial direct-current stimulation (tDCS) over the rDLPFC to reexamine its causal role in regulating self-interested behavior among ultimatum game responders. In addition, we tested whether this manipulation promotes responses to both intentional unfairness and inequality resulting from an intention-free process. The results show that anodal stimulation increased rejection rates of unfair offers, regardless of whether they were proposed by a human partner or randomly generated by a computer. These findings suggest that rDLPFC activity supports the implementation of social preferences more broadly, promoting both reciprocal fairness and inequality aversion. When considered alongside prior findings demonstrating an opposite effect of anodal stimulation applied to an adjacent lateral prefrontal region using a similar paradigm, the results point to distinct and complementary roles of lateral prefrontal regions in managing the conflict between self-interest and social preferences. We discuss implications for dual-process accounts of social decision-making.
